speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Judiciary is widely recognised as being amongst the most efficient and responsive judiciaries globally, dispensing justice with independence, integrity and impartiality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The visibility of the Singapore Judiciary has increased over the years, especially with the launch of the Singapore International Commercial Court in 2015.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our Judiciary is also a progressive one which continually looks to anticipate future developments in the legal industry and profession.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is evident from the various Judiciary-led initiatives and reforms, such as collaboration between the Family Justice Courts and the Singapore Mediation Centre, to provide parties with more options to settle their family disputes amicably, the reforms to the medical litigation process, and leading the charge for the increasing use of technology in the way law is practised and justice dispensed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I quote from a Canadian case: " he object of the law in requiring an oath is to get at the truth relative to matters in dispute by getting a hold on the conscience of the witness." The current Oaths and Declarations Act, when it was first enacted in 2000, combined what was previously the Oaths Act, the Oaths of Office and Allegiance Act and the Statutory Declarations Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 4 of the Act allows persons giving evidence to take an oath.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is noteworthy that the original Oaths Act enacted in 1890 contained a provision which allowed a person to give evidence on oath "in any form common amongst or held binding by persons of the race or persuasion to which he belongs, and not repugnant to justice or decency".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may be viewed as a technical point but, in my respectful view, is nonetheless an important symbolic point that is in keeping with our nation's values and better serve the objective behind the taking of the oath that I outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also accords with the practice in major common law jurisdictions, such as Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, the UK Oaths Act 1978 expressly enables persons of all faiths to take either oaths or affirmations as they see fit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Pillai correctly pointed out that the current practice in our Courts allows Christians to take oaths by swearing on the Bible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a long-established practice which can be traced back to the UK tradition, which we adopted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Making an affirmation is, therefore, not an exception to the general rule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Seen in this context, our current practice of taking oath is really a historical exception.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Pillai has suggested that it may be possible to update the current practice of taking oaths, such that people of all religions can take oaths in accordance with their religious beliefs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, there are practical issues with Mr Pillai's suggestion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A move to change the current practice of taking oaths may also invite a multitude of claims from people of different religious beliefs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Pillai, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.51 pm until 5.10 pm.
